title: What might have been
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The imperfect subjunctive is one cheap rule: take the third-person plural preterite, drop -ron, add -ra. hablaron becomes hablara, comieron comiera, pudieron pudiera, supieron supiera, dijeron dijera. There are no exceptions worth naming.

A past hypothesis has two slots and two different verbs. The si-clause takes hubiera plus a participle; the other clause takes habría plus a participle. Si hubiera sabido, habría venido. Neither verb may do the other's job.

English would have is one auxiliary covering both halves, so a learner levels the Spanish and writes Si habría sabido. It is said in some regions and it is still heard as an error across the language, so this course writes hubiera in the si-clause and nothing else.

ojalá is the one Spanish word that takes the subjunctive with no clause around it. With the imperfect subjunctive it wishes about now (Ojalá pudiera); with hubiera plus a participle it wishes about the past (Ojalá me lo hubieras dicho).

debería haber and tenía que haber are ordinary conjugated verbs plus haber plus a participle, not frozen modals. The person sits on debería and tenía; haber never changes and the participle never agrees.

The -se twin (hablase, supiese, hubiese) is the same tense spelled another way, commoner in Spain and in writing. Read it and expect it; write -ara and -iera, which is what this course teaches and what is understood everywhere.

The feeling words around a regret — menos mal que, qué pena, me arrepiento de — take an ordinary indicative clause or an infinitive, never the subjunctive. The subjunctive of emotion is not L4's, and this module does not open it.

sentences.display: Si hubiera sabido, habría venido a la fiesta.
sentences.cue: If I had known, I would have come to the party.

words.note: The si-half of a past hypothesis: hubiera plus a participle. It is the imperfect subjunctive of haber, built by rule 1, and habría can never stand in this slot.
The participle of saber. Si hubiera sabido is the whole thought in Spanish where English says if I had known: the object is normally left out.
The other half: habría plus a participle says what would then have happened. Same conditional endings as L3-M4's iría and podría.
The participle of venir. habría venido is would have come, two Spanish words for two English ones, and the participle never agrees.

sentences.trap: English would have does both halves at once. Spanish uses two different verbs: hubiera in the si-clause, habría in the other. One verb doing both jobs is the error a learner makes first.
sentences.sound: see oo-BYEH-ra sa-BEE-do, a-BREE-a be-NEE-do. The h is silent in both auxiliaries, and the b of habría and the v of venido are the same sound.

variations.display: Si hubieras sabido, habrías venido a la fiesta.
variations.cue: If you had known, you would have come to the party.

variations.display: Si hubiera sabido, habría venido antes.
variations.cue: If I had known, I would have come earlier.

mistake.display: Si habría sabido, habría venido a la fiesta.
mistake.why: habría cannot open the si-clause. The hypothesis takes hubiera; only the consequence takes habría.

sentences.usage: Said to a friend who did not tell you what was on. Regrets are said to people you are close to, so the scene is tú all through this module.
sentences.mnemonic: si takes hubiera, the other half takes habría — two halves, two verbs.

sentences.display: Si me hubieras avisado, te habría esperado en casa.
sentences.cue: If you had let me know, I would have waited for you at home.

words.note: The participle of avisar, the ordinary verb for letting somebody know. avisar a alguien is what you ask of a person who is going to be late.
The participle of esperar, L2-M1's verb. esperar covers both wait and wait for with no preposition at all: te habría esperado.

sentences.trap: English needs for — I would have waited FOR you. Spanish esperar takes the person straight, as a plain object: te habría esperado.
sentences.sound: see me oo-BYEH-ras a-bee-SA-do. The s of esperado is the plain hissing s, never the z sound English puts in the middle of easy.

variations.display: Si me hubieras avisado, habría esperado en casa.
variations.cue: If you had let me know, I would have waited at home.
variations.changed: the person waited for is left out

variations.display: Si me hubieras avisado, te habría esperado en la fiesta.
variations.cue: If you had let me know, I would have waited for you at the party.
variations.changed: where the waiting would have happened

mistake.display: Si me habrías avisado, te habría esperado en casa.
mistake.why: The si-clause takes hubieras. habrías belongs only in the other half of the sentence.

sentences.usage: A mild reproach between friends, and the commonest regret there is. Neutral across Spain and Latin America.
sentences.mnemonic: The warning comes first in life and hubieras comes first in the sentence.

sentences.display: Ojalá pudiera cambiar lo que dije aquel día.
sentences.cue: I wish I could change what I said that day.

words.note: The one Spanish word that takes the subjunctive with no clause around it. From Arabic, and stressed on the last syllable: o-kha-LA.

words.cue: could (as a wish or a hypothesis)
words.note: Imperfect subjunctive of poder, built the module's way: pudieron minus -ron plus -ra. L3-M4 bought the conditional podría; this is its partner.
A regular -ar verb, here in the bare infinitive after pudiera. Spanish stacks the infinitive straight onto the modal with nothing in between.
The far demonstrative. ese día is that day; aquel día is that day back then. Regret reaches for aquel because the day cannot be got back.

sentences.trap: English I wish I could is a verb plus a modal. Spanish has one word, ojalá, and it hands the whole job to the mood that follows it.
sentences.sound: o-kha-LA poo-DYEH-ra. The j of ojalá is the rough h made at the back of the throat, and the stress lands on the final a.

variations.display: Ojalá pudiera cambiar lo que dije aquella noche.
variations.cue: I wish I could change what I said that night.

variations.display: Ojalá pudiéramos cambiar lo que dije aquel día.
variations.cue: I wish we could change what I said that day.

mistake.display: Ojalá puedo cambiar lo que dije aquel día.
mistake.why: ojalá never takes the indicative. The subjunctive is the whole point of the word, so puedo has to become pudiera.

sentences.usage: Said about something already done and not fixable. ojalá plus the imperfect subjunctive is the everyday regret in Spain and Latin America alike.
sentences.mnemonic: ojalá never speaks the indicative — it only ever wishes.

sentences.display: Si me hubieras escuchado, no habría pasado nada.
sentences.cue: If you had listened to me, nothing would have happened.

words.note: The participle of escuchar. Like esperar it takes the person straight: me hubieras escuchado, with no Spanish word for to.
The participle of pasar. no habría pasado nada is the fixed way to say nothing would have happened, and the no in front is not optional.

sentences.trap: Spanish keeps both negatives when nada follows the verb: no habría pasado nada. Dropping the first one gives habría pasado nada, which is not Spanish at all.
sentences.sound: es-koo-CHA-do. The ch is the ch of church, and in fast speech the final -ado is often heard as -ao.

variations.display: Si me hubieras escuchado, nada habría pasado.
variations.cue: If you had listened to me, nothing would have happened.
variations.changed: nada moves in front, so the first no disappears

variations.display: Si te hubiera escuchado, no habría pasado nada.
variations.cue: If I had listened to you, nothing would have happened.

mistake.display: Si me hubieras escuchado, habría pasado nada.
mistake.why: With nada after the verb the no is required: no habría pasado nada. Spanish negates twice and means it once.

sentences.usage: A reproach with a soft edge, said after the fact and usually with a shrug. Between friends and inside a family.
sentences.mnemonic: nada after the verb drags a no in front of it.

sentences.display: Ojalá supiera qué decir en una fiesta.
sentences.cue: I wish I knew what to say at a party.

words.note: Imperfect subjunctive of saber: supieron minus -ron plus -ra. L3-M2 taught sé for reporting; this is the same verb wishing.
The bare infinitive. qué decir is what to say: Spanish uses the plain infinitive where English needs to plus a verb.

sentences.trap: English what to say carries no subject and no tense, and neither does qué decir. The accent on qué stays, because it is still the question word underneath.
sentences.sound: o-kha-LA soo-PYEH-ra. Stress falls on PYEH, and the u is a real oo, never the English yoo of usual.

variations.display: Ojalá supieras qué decir en una fiesta.
variations.cue: I wish you knew what to say at a party.

variations.display: Ojalá supiera qué decir ahora.
variations.cue: I wish I knew what to say now.

mistake.display: Ojalá sé qué decir en una fiesta.
mistake.why: ojalá takes the subjunctive. sé is the indicative and cannot follow it, however ordinary the wish.

sentences.usage: The line a learner actually needs: said about small talk, about a hard conversation, about any moment the words did not come.

sentences.display: Deberías haber llamado antes de la fiesta.
sentences.cue: You should have called before the party.

words.note: The conditional of deber. With haber plus a participle it is should have — a conjugated verb where English uses a modal with no tense of its own.
The participle of llamar, the verb L1-M1 bought in Me llamo. llamar is both to call somebody by name and to ring them.

sentences.trap: English should have is one frozen modal. Spanish conjugates the first word: debería haber for I, deberías haber for you. haber itself never moves.
sentences.sound: de-be-REE-as a-BER lya-MA-do. The double ll is the y of yes in most of the Spanish-speaking world.

variations.display: Debería haber llamado antes de la fiesta.
variations.cue: I should have called before the party.

variations.display: Deberías haber llamado antes.
variations.cue: You should have called earlier.
variations.changed: how much is said about when

mistake.display: Deberías haber llamando antes de la fiesta.
mistake.why: haber takes the participle llamado. llamando is the gerund and never follows haber.

sentences.usage: A gentle telling-off between friends. To somebody you address as usted it would be debería haber llamado, with the same two words after it.
sentences.mnemonic: debería carries the person, haber carries the past.

sentences.display: Tenía que haber salido de casa mucho antes.
sentences.cue: I should have left the house much earlier.

words.note: Indexed as two words, because L3-M5 owns bare tenía. With haber plus a participle it is the heavier regret: a duty that was owed, not merely good advice.
The infinitive of the auxiliary, and it never changes: debería haber, tenía que haber, no haber dicho. Everything after it is a participle.
The participle of salir, L3-M10's verb. salir de casa is to leave the house, and the de is not optional in Spanish.

sentences.trap: tenía que haber salido and debería haber salido are both should have left, but tenía que carries an obligation that was owed. English collapses the two; Spanish keeps them apart.
sentences.sound: te-NEE-a ke a-BER sa-LEE-do. haber and a ver sound identical in speech, and only the spelling tells them apart.

variations.display: Tenías que haber salido de casa mucho antes.
variations.cue: You should have left the house much earlier.

variations.display: Tenía que haber salido de casa antes.
variations.cue: I should have left the house earlier.

mistake.display: Tenía que haber salir de casa mucho antes.
mistake.why: haber takes a participle, salido, and never a second infinitive.

sentences.usage: Said about a train missed or a meeting reached late. It sounds harder on the speaker than debería haber, which is why it is the one people use on themselves.
sentences.mnemonic: tenía que haber is the duty; debería haber is the advice.

sentences.display: Ojalá me lo hubieras dicho ayer por la mañana.
sentences.cue: I wish you had told me yesterday morning.

words.note: The participle of decir, and irregular: dicho, never decido. It is the one participle in this module that rule 1 cannot build for you.

sentences.trap: ojalá plus hubiera plus a participle wishes about the PAST. ojalá plus a plain imperfect subjunctive, as in S03 and S05, wishes about now. The auxiliary is what moves the wish backwards.
sentences.sound: o-kha-LA me lo oo-BYEH-ras DEE-cho. me lo runs together in one breath before the verb, exactly as L4-M1 taught it.

variations.display: Ojalá me lo hubieras dicho antes.
variations.cue: I wish you had told me earlier.
variations.changed: when it should have been said

variations.display: Ojalá me lo hubiera dicho ayer por la mañana.
variations.cue: I wish he had told me yesterday morning.

mistake.display: Ojalá me lo habrías dicho ayer por la mañana.
mistake.why: ojalá takes the subjunctive, so hubieras. habrías is the conditional and belongs in the other half of a si-sentence.

sentences.usage: The past wish, and the one that carries the most feeling. Said to somebody close, about news that reached you too late.
sentences.mnemonic: ojalá + hubiera looks backwards; ojalá + pudiera looks at now.

sentences.display: Menos mal que no dije nada aquella noche.
sentences.cue: Just as well I didn't say anything that night.

words.note: Two words, one meaning: relief at what did NOT happen. It takes que plus an ordinary indicative clause and never the subjunctive.
Feminine: la noche, aquella noche. por la noche is at night; de noche is by night, said of the way something is done.

sentences.trap: menos mal que is a relief, not a regret, and it is the one frame in this module that keeps the indicative. dije stays as it is: no subjunctive follows it.
sentences.sound: MEH-nos MAL ke. The two words run together as one, and the que is a plain ke with no w sound.

variations.display: Menos mal que no dije nada en la fiesta.
variations.cue: Just as well I didn't say anything at the party.

variations.display: Menos mal que no dije nada.
variations.cue: Just as well I didn't say anything.

mistake.display: Menos mal que no dijera nada aquella noche.
mistake.why: menos mal que takes the indicative. dijera is the subjunctive and belongs after si or ojalá, not here.

sentences.usage: The other side of the module: the regret that did not have to be had. Extremely common in speech, and it needs no verb of its own.
sentences.mnemonic: menos mal keeps the indicative — relief is a fact, not a wish.

sentences.display: Me arrepiento de no haber dicho la verdad.
sentences.cue: I regret not having told the truth.

words.note: Always reflexive and always followed by de. What comes after is an infinitive: de no haber dicho, with the no sitting in front of haber.

sentences.trap: English regret takes an -ing form: regret not saying. Spanish takes the perfect infinitive instead, de no haber dicho, and the no goes before haber rather than before the participle.
sentences.sound: me a-rre-PYEN-to. The rr is trilled, and the trill is the whole difference between this word and a single-r one.

variations.display: Me arrepiento de no haber llamado antes.
variations.cue: I regret not having called earlier.

variations.display: Me arrepiento de haber dicho la verdad.
variations.cue: I regret having told the truth.
variations.changed: the regret is turned around — the no is gone

mistake.display: Me arrepiento que no dije la verdad.
mistake.why: arrepentirse drags de behind it, and a perfect infinitive follows: me arrepiento de no haber dicho.

sentences.usage: The heaviest of the module's regrets and the least casual. In ordinary speech Spanish reaches for ojalá or qué pena far more often.
sentences.mnemonic: arrepentirse always drags de behind it.
